data.notes:
Vasili Sergeyevich Oshchepkov (1893-1938) was a Soviet martial artist and one of the three founders of SAMBO (along with Anatoly Kharlampiyev and Viktor Spiridonov).
He studied judo under Jigoro Kano at the Kodokan in Tokyo from 1911 to 1917, becoming the first Russian to earn a black belt in judo.
He was awarded 1st dan in June 1913 and 2nd dan in October 1917, becoming the first Russian and third European to achieve this rank.
Oshchepkov played a key role in developing SAMBO by combining judo techniques with traditional Russian wrestling styles.
He served as a military intelligence officer and was arrested during the Great Purge, executed on October 10, 1938.
He was posthumously rehabilitated in 1957 and recognized for his contributions to Soviet martial arts.

Anatoliy Solomonovich Rakhlin (1938-2013) was a prominent Soviet and Russian SAMBO and judo coach.
He is best known as the childhood trainer of Vladimir Putin, who began training with him at age 11 in 1965.
Rakhlin trained Putin for 11 years, helping him achieve Master of Sports ranks in both SAMBO and judo.
He was the head coach of the "Trud" sports society in Leningrad/Saint Petersburg.
He held the 8th dan rank in judo and was an Honorary Coach of the Russian Federation.
He continued to maintain a close relationship with Putin throughout his life, being invited to important personal and state events.

data.notes:
As relações de aprendizagem entre os membros fundadores da UBU não
são claras, provavelmente apenas por não serem tópico que é
expressamente dito nas fontes, mas também provavelmente pela
dinâmica de grande voluntarismo e inovação que caracterizam uma
organização que foi pioneira. Uma leitura transversal das várias
fontes apontam para relações de aprendizagem mútua, com posterior
validação/homologação em alguns casos (como no do Karate).  Assim,
a identificação das relações aluno/professor provavelmente
demonstrarão uma relação em rede, sendo que a figura de Corrêa
Pereira se apresenta como agregadora, mesmo não sendo na maior
parte das vezes claro a influência directa (em termos de treino)
que existiu, em especial a partir do final dos anos 50.  Isto é
particularmente aplicável ao Judo (e jujutsu), visto que para o
Aikido e Karate a evolução posterior na UBU permitem leituras mais
concretas. Sobre o Judo, antes de Shirooka não é claro quem faz a
instrução, assumindo-se que Corrêa Pereira é uma das fontes (e.g.,
a demonstração com Sebastião Durão).

data.notes:
José da Costa Branco (born March 13, 1937 in Lourenço Marques, Mozambique) is a Portuguese judoka and shooting champion. 
He began judo in Mozambique at the Clube de Judo de Lourenço Marques. After moving to Portugal following the independence of Mozambique, he joined Judo Clube de Portugal in 1975 where he became a student of Kiyoshi Kobayashi. 
He represented Portugal at the 1980 Moscow Olympics in the -65kg category, winning one match and losing one. He was part of a small Portuguese delegation of only 11 athletes due to the US-led boycott of the Games.
According to his own account in interviews, Kobayashi was a crucial mentor during a difficult period in his life after relocating from Mozambique.
He also became a national shooting champion in Portugal, demonstrating versatility across different sports.
His 3rd dan rank was documented in the 1983 book "Judo: da iniciação à competição" published by Centelha.

data.notes: José Manuel da Silva Araújo (born 1955 in Lisbon) is a Portuguese aikido practitioner who started training at age 10 in 1966 at Academia de Budo. He is considered one of the earliest Portuguese aikido practitioners still active. In his 2000 interview with Pedro Escudeiro, he stated that he began with aikido under Carlos Pereira (student of Georges Stobbaerts) and karate under Fragoso Fernandes (student of Luís Pires Martins). He later trained with Leopoldo Ferreira from 1973. He has been involved with União Portuguesa de Budo and is listed as a professor at Universidade da Beira Interior (UBI), though the UBU profile page returns a 404 error. According to the interview, he considers himself "o praticante português de Aikido mais antigo, actualmente em actividade" (the oldest Portuguese aikido practitioner currently active).

data.notes:
Full name: Henrique Carinhas Martins Nunes. Born in Benguela, Angola (then Portuguese colony). 
Started judo in 1954 with Afonso Henriques Maia Loureiro. Became student of Kiyoshi Kobayashi in 1959 when Kobayashi arrived in Portugal. 
National champion multiple times (first championship medal in 1966 from Kobayashi). Known for extensive collection of judo materials (videos, books, magazines) referred to as his "santuário do judo" (judo sanctuary). 
Described Kiyoshi Kobayashi as "the Nureyev of standing judo" for his elegance and technical precision. 
Has expressed concern about modern judo teaching methods and commercialization. 8th dan awarded in 2019.

data.notes: Fernando Costa Matos was born in Ponta Delgada, Azores in 1941. He began practicing judo in 1959 at INEF with Kiyoshi Kobayashi, who is considered the father of Portuguese judo. He started training at Judo Clube de Portugal in 1961. He was the first Portuguese judoka to compete in the Olympics, participating in Tokyo 1964 where he also served as Portugal's flag bearer. He later trained in Japan for two years. His competitive career included European Championships in 1963. He served as national team coach for the 1972 and 1992 Olympics. He was president of the Portuguese Judo Federation and received the 9th dan in 2019 at the FPJ 60th anniversary gala. He was also a multi-sport athlete, practicing swimming, sailing, rowing, water polo, handball, and football in his youth.

- Founder and head of Takemusu Aikido Carlos Portas (TACP), an independent aikido school in Aveiro.

sources.quotation: Mestre António Corrêa Pereira (1906-1982). Fundador da Academia de Judo (1946) e da Academia de Budo (1958). Fundador da União Portuguesa de Budo. Professor de Judo e Budo. Introdutor do Judo Marcial em Portugal.

A União Portuguesa de Budo, a mais antiga associação de Artes Marciais em Portugal, foi fundada pelo Mestre António Hilmar Schalck Corrêa Pereira. Iniciado na prática do Ju-Jutsu em Berlim, na década de trinta, quando estudava engenharia química na Universidade Técnica de Berlim. Funda então a Academia de Judo, cujo Dojo funcionará na Rua de S. Paulo até à abertura, em 1958, do Dojo de Entrecampos, que passa a chamar-se "Academia de Budo".

António Correia Pereira foi o editor da primeira revista sobre Judo Kodokan publicada em Portugal, da qual apenas saíram nove números. Sob o pseudónimo de Minero publicou o livro intitulado «A Essência do Judo». Foi o primeiro cinto negro português inscrito no Kodokan, porém por nunca ter estado ligado à Federação Portuguesa de Judo a sua graduação não é reconhecida por aquela entidade.

data.notes:
As relações de aprendizagem entre os membros fundadores da UBU não
são claras, provavelmente apenas por não serem tópico que é
expressamente dito nas fontes, mas também provavelmente pela
dinâmica de grande voluntarismo e inovação que caracterizam uma
organização que foi pioneira. Uma leitura transversal das várias
fontes apontam para relações de aprendizagem mútua, com posterior
validação/homologação em alguns casos (como no do Karate).  Assim,
a identificação das relações aluno/professor provavelmente
demonstrarão uma relação em rede, sendo que a figura de Corrêa
Pereira se apresenta como agregadora, mesmo não sendo na maior
parte das vezes claro a influência directa (em termos de treino)
que existiu, em especial a partir do final dos anos 50.  Isto é
particularmente aplicável ao Judo (e jujutsu), visto que para o
Aikido e Karate a evolução posterior na UBU permitem leituras mais
concretas. Sobre o Judo, antes de Shirooka não é claro quem faz a
instrução, assumindo-se que Corrêa Pereira é uma das fontes (e.g.
a demonstração com Sebastião Durão). O 1º dan Kodokan é dado como
atribuido na Alemanha (Figueiredo 2006), em entrevista Luis
Antunes indica que Corrêa Pereira treinou Jujutsu em Berlim com
Eric Rahm (buscas no dasjudoforum indicam que esta hipótese não é descabida).

data.notes:
José Alexandre Gueifão nasceu em Lisboa em 7 de dezembro de 1940 e faleceu em 24 de julho de 2025.
Iniciou-se na prática de judo em 1960 e no karate em 1964, sendo co-introdutor do karate em Portugal.
Fundador da Suishinkan Portugal, foi presidente da Associação Shotokai de Portugal (1999-2006) e membro do Conselho de Graduações da ASP.
Teve dois filhos, incluindo Pedro Gueifão (4º dan de karate Shotokai).
Participou em numerosos estágios com mestres japoneses incluindo Tetsuji Murakami, Shigeru Egami, Motohiro Yanagisawa, Yoshiharu Takisawa, Yoshinori Takita e Hidemitsu Nakao.
Foi professor de judo no Colégio Militar sob orientação do Tenente Coronel Freire de Almeida.
Possuiu diversas certificações incluindo Curso de Formação para Agentes do Ensino de 2º Grau pela CDAM, Curso de Treinador de Karate Nível III pela FNK-P, e Curso de Treinador de Desporto Karate Grau 4 pelo IPDJ.

description.en: Ueda Heitaro (1877-1949) was a Japanese kendo master, three-time participant in the Tenran shiai (imperial martial arts tournaments), and the only kenshi to be deified as a Shinto kami. description.en: Ryōhei Uchida (内田 良平, Uchida Ryōhei, 11 February 1873 – 26 July 1937) was a Japanese ultranationalist political theorist, Pan-Asianist, and martial artist, active in the pre-war Empire of Japan. He was also an accomplished jūdōka, a favorite of Kanō shihan 師範 (master), one of the three most senior 5th dan rank holders in Kodokan history, and a noted street brawler.  He was the son of Shinto Muso-ryu practitioner Uchida Ryōgorō, and from an early age was interested in many forms of Japanese traditional martial arts, including kyūdō, kendo, judo and sumo.
description.ja: 内田 良平（うちだ りょうへい、1874年〈明治7年〉2月11日 - 1937年 〈昭和12年〉7月26日）は、日本の国家主義者・右翼運動家・アジア主 義者。黒龍会主幹、大日本生産党総裁。 旧福岡藩士であり、武芸の達 人として知られた内田良五郎の三男として現在の福岡県福岡市大円寺町 （現・唐人町）に生まれる[1]。幼名良助、のち甲（きのえ）。明治34 年（1902年）に良平と改名した。幼時より弓道、剣道、柔術、相撲、射 撃を父に学んだ。なお、父・良五郎の神道夢想流杖術の門下には、[2] 「昭和の剣聖」の一人である中山博道がいる。

description.en: Japanese aikido master, student of Morihiro Saito and Morihei Ueshiba, founder of Aïki Shin Myo Den (Takemusu Aiki)

data.notes:
- Born in Ibaraki Prefecture, Japan
- First visited Iwama in 1962 and decided to follow the teaching of Morihei Ueshiba and his assistant Morihiro Saito
- Became Morihiro Saito's uchideshi (live-in student) in 1968 and was adopted by the Saito family
- Practiced at Iwama Dojo for about 7 years, studying under both Ueshiba (until his death in April 1969) and Saito

data.notes:
Yoshio Sugino (1904-1998) was a prominent Japanese martial artist and film choreographer known for his expertise in multiple martial arts and his work on historical films.

**Early Life and Education:**
- Born in Naruto village, Chiba prefecture, in December 1904
- Family moved to Tokyo when he was young
- Enrolled at Keio University in 1918, where he joined multiple martial arts clubs including judo, kendo, sumo, and kyudo

**Judo Career:**
- Studied judo under Kunisaburo Iizuka at Keio University (1918-1919)
- Achieved 4th dan in judo by 1927, remaining undefeated until earning this rank
- Known for techniques like utsurigoshi (hip shift), urawaza (rear techniques), and kaeshiwaza (reversals)
- His friend Minoru Mochizuki commented: "Sugino? That guy has the kami [divine] in him!"

**Katori Shinto-ryu Training:**
- Introduced to Katori Shinto-ryu by Jigoro Kano in 1927
- Trained under four dispatched shihan: Narimichi Tamai, Sozaemon Kuboki, Tanekichi Ito, and Ichizo Shiina
- These shihan taught at the Kodokan and also trained Sugino in Kawasaki on Sundays and Mondays
- Studied the complete curriculum including sword, iai, bo, naginata, yari, shuriken, and ryoto (two-sword) techniques

**Aikido Training:**
- Met Morihei Ueshiba in early 1930s (around 1931-1932)
- Received aikido teaching license in 1935
- Opened an Aikikai-affiliated dojo in 1935, which became the second Aikikai branch dojo in Japan
- Ueshiba and his son Kisshomaru would teach at Sugino's dojo once a month

**Yoshin Koryu Training:**
- Studied Yoshin Koryu jujutsu under Genro Kanaya starting around 1928
- Reached kyoshi level (between renshi and hanshi) in the style by 1938
- Demonstrated Yoshin Koryu at the Imperial Palace around 1937-1938

**Film Career:**
- Provided sword instruction for Akira Kurosawa's "Seven Samurai" (1954)
- Also worked as fencing instructor for Kurosawa's "Hidden Fortress" and "Yojimbo"
- Did choreography for Hiroshi Inagaki's "Samurai Trilogy"
- Known for realistic fight choreography that departed from earlier Kabuki-influenced styles

**Personal Life and Dojo:**
- Opened his first dojo (Kodokan Judo Shugyojo) in Kawasaki in 1927
- Ran a bone-setting clinic from his dojo, treating war-wounded after WWII
- Married twice, had multiple children
- Known for his loud voice and strict teaching style
- Wore a long beard to appear more distinguished (was nicknamed "Prince Regent" for resemblance to Prince Regent Hirohito)

**Later Years:**
- In 1995, at age 92, underwent successful surgery to save his arm from amputation after an artery blockage
- Continued teaching until his death in 1998 at age 93
- Remembered as one of the last living witnesses to classical Japanese martial arts traditions

**Philosophy:**
- Believed "Budo is kata. Kata training is everything in budo."
- Viewed modern judo as having become "nothing but a sport" with weight categories and modifications
- Valued the classical traditions for their depth and principles

Sugino's life spanned nearly the entire 20th century and he trained with many of Japan's most legendary martial artists, making him a crucial link in the transmission of classical martial arts knowledge.

data.notes: Shingai Tadaatsu was born on March 1, 1842, in the Edo residence of the Ōgaki Domain as the seventh son of samurai Shingai Yoshizō. At age 12, he entered Kubota-ha Tamiya-ryū under Shimamura Yūyū. He lost both parents at age 17 and worked as a servant while continuing sword training. He eventually surpassed his teacher and took the name 'Torao' (寅雄), borrowing one character from his teacher's name. During the Boshin War, he fought with the Ōgaki Domain and later joined the Owari Domain's 'Return to Righteousness Corps', where he contracted syphilis which caused his nose to collapse (earning him the nickname 'Noseless Shingai'). After the war, he became a sword instructor at the Owari Domain's Meirinkan school. After the abolition of domains, he made a living through sword exhibitions. Around 1882-1883, he became a sword instructor for the Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department. He later served as a kendo instructor for the Imperial Household Agency Police, Gakushūin, and Keio University. In 1908, he was awarded the rank of hanshi by the Dai Nippon Butoku Kai and served on the committee that established the Dai Nippon Teikoku Kendō Kata. Along with Negishi Shingorō and Tokuno Kaneshirō, he was called one of the 'Three Elders of Eastern Capital Kendo'. He was known as 'Kote-giri Shingai' (Shingai the Wrist-Cutter) for his skill at striking the kote (wrist) and 'Hana-kake Shingai' (Noseless Shingai) due to his collapsed nose from syphilis. In his later years, he was invited to the Kōnishī Brewery's dōjō Shūbukan, where he helped establish the Shūbukan Okunokata along with Tomiyama En (Jikishinkage-ryū) and Midamura Kengyō (Tendō-ryū). He died on February 9, 1920, from a cerebral hemorrhage while on his way to the Imperial Household Agency Police dōjō Saimeikan. His grave is at Aoyama Cemetery.

description.en: Soshihiro Satake (佐竹信四郎), also known as Antônio Satake, was a Japanese-born Brazilian martial artist and teacher. One of the primary founders of Brazilian jiu-jitsu (BJJ), he pioneered judo in Brazil, the United Kingdom, and other countries. He was a member of the Ten'gu Club sports social group.

data.notes: Soshihiro Satake was a Japanese-born Brazilian martial artist and teacher. He started as a sumo wrestler before joining the Kodokan dojo academy in May 1892. He graduated from Waseda University in 1904 and was a member of the Ten'gu Club sports social group. Together with Mitsuyo Maeda, he formed the head of the second generation of Kodokan judoka. In 1904, he traveled to the United States with Tsunejiro Tomita and Maeda, arriving in New York City on December 8, 1904. He traveled extensively throughout the Americas and Europe, including Cuba where he was known as one of the 'Four Kings of Cuba' along with Maeda, Akitaro Ono, and Tokugoro Ito. He settled in Mexico for a time, teaching judo at military academies and establishing a sock manufacturing business in Mexico City. He returned to Japan in 1934 and died on May 11, 1936, at approximately 55 years of age. His grave is at Rinsen-ji temple in Aoyama, Tokyo. He is considered one of the primary founders of Brazilian jiu-jitsu and pioneered judo in Brazil, the United Kingdom, and other countries.

data.notes: Morihiro Saito was a teacher of the Japanese martial art of aikido, with many students around the world. Saito's practice of aikido spanned 56 years, from the age of 18, when he first met aikido founder Morihei Ueshiba, until his death in 2002. He was born in Ibaraki Prefecture, Japan, on March 31, 1928, and died of cancer on May 13, 2002 in Iwama, Ibaraki Prefecture. Saito trained under Ueshiba for 23 years and after Ueshiba's passing, became the head of the Iwama Dojo and keeper of the Aiki Shrine. He is renowned for his depth of technical knowledge and dissemination of Aikido weapons, having trained in Aikido for more than 50 years and regarded as the world's technical expert on Aikido. Key figure in 1886 Tokyo Metropolitan Police tournament where Kodokan judo defeated Totsuka-ha Yoshin-ryu jujutsu, establishing judo's superiority. Known for yama arashi technique and exceptional agility, nicknamed 'Cat' for ability to land on feet when thrown. Left Kodokan in 1890 after street brawl incident. Later worked as journalist in Nagasaki for 'Toyo Hinode Shimbun', taught judo, kyudo, and Japanese swimming. Died in Onomichi in 1922. Model for main character in Tomita Tsuneo's novel 'Sugata Sanshiro' (1942), adapted into Akira Kurosawa's 1943 film.

data.notes: Oshima Masateru (also known as Oshima Ichigaku Masateru) was the 7th Soke of Edo-line Yagyu Shingan-ryū Taijutsu (Araki-do). He taught Yagyu-ryu bojutsu to a young Jigoro Kano, as documented in Kano's own writings. He was a member of the Shinsengumi and, with the assistance of Yamaoka Tesshu, opened a dojo in Tokyo during the Meiji era to teach the style. He succeeded Goto Yagyu-sai (not in database) and taught Hoshino Tenchi, who was active in the Meiji literary world and taught women's martial arts at Meiji Girls' School. The Edo transmission of his teachings was later passed to the Hokuriku region, but its current whereabouts are unknown.

description.en: Ogawa Kinnosuke was born in 1884 in Aichi prefecture. He began kendo whilst in school, at around 13/15 years of age, under kendo hanshi Kato Kiichi and later under Kohori Yasutada. He was a student and later an instructor at the Budo Senmon Gakko, as well as in the Nagoya police. He was a Butokukai hanshi and was Busen's principle kendo instructor in the 1930's and up until 1945.  He authored "Teikoku Kendo Kyohon" (The Kendo Textbook of Imperial Japan) in 1932 (revised 1937) and was posthumously inducted into the Kendo Hall of Fame in 2003.

description.ja: 宮川太一郎、名は鍜キタウ。筑前の人。嘉永元年七月二十四日福岡に生 る。世、黒田氏に仕へ、其の藩士たり。夙に文武館に入り、専ら武技を 講修し、撃剣（一刀流）柔術（自得天心流）の奥技を究む。維新後藩の 併心隊に入り、青年派の牛耳を執る。明治三年、事を以て就義隊の領袖 箱田六輔等と争ひ、屏居を命ぜらる。後、節を折り、六輔、及、進藤喜 平太等と共に、高場乱の門に入る。七年二月、佐賀の変、福岡臨時鎮撫 隊の組織せらるゝや、太一郎、六輔と共に、其半隊長たり。八年、六輔、 及、頭山満等と矯志社を起し、九年十二月、萩の事変に坐せられて、六 輔等と共に獄に下り、十一年三月、始めて釈さる。後、開墾社を博多向 浜に開き、爾来志を政治上に断ち、専ら実業に従事す。 宮川太一郎嘉永元年（1848）生正林又七郎の高弟・免許皆伝代々黒田家 の臣である。一万流剣術，自剛天真流組討を極め，明治10年(1877) 11 月玄洋社附属の向浜塾で自聞天真流を教授したのが，後の明道館道場の 起源とされている。大正9年(1920)6月20日77才にて病没。長男．宮川彦 之助も目録まで進み，自剛天真流の普及に務めた。

description.en: Mikinosuke Kawaishi (川石 酒造之助, Kawaishi Mikinosuke, born 13 August 1899 – 30 January 1969) was a Japanese master of jujutsu and judo who achieved the rank of 7th Dan. He led the development of Judo in France, with Shozo Awazu, and much of Europe and is credited with introducing the colored belt system for differentiating early grades. However, written accounts from the archives of London's Budokwai judo club, founded in 1918, record the use of colored judo belts at the 1926 9th annual Budokwai Display, and a list of ranked colored judokas appears in the Budokwai Committee Minutes of June 1927. Kawaishi visited London and the Budokwai in 1928, and was probably inspired to bring the colored belt system to France. The Fédération Française posthumously awarded him 10th Dan in judo and jujutsu.

description.en: Jigoro Kano (嘉納 治五郎, 10 December 1860 – 4 May 1938[3]) was a Japanese educator, athlete, and the founder of Judo. Along with Ju-Jutsu, Judo was one of the first Japanese martial arts to gain widespread international recognition, and the first to become an official Olympic sport. Pedagogical innovations attributed to Kanō include the use of black and white belts, and the introduction of dan ranking to show the relative ranking among members of a martial art style. Well-known mottoes attributed to Kanō include "good use of energy" (精力善用 seiryoku zen'yō) and "mutual welfare and benefit" (自他共栄 jita kyōei).
description.ja: 嘉納 治五郎（かのう じごろう、万延元年10月28日〈1860年12月10日〉-昭 和13年〈1938年〉5月4日）は、日本の柔道家・教育者・貴族院議員。兵 庫県出身。別表記：加納治五郎[1]。講道館柔道の創始者であり[2]、柔 道・スポーツ・教育分野の発展や日本のオリンピック初参加に尽力する など、明治から昭和にかけて日本におけるスポーツの道を開いた。「柔 道の父」と呼ばれ、また、「日本の体育の父」とも称される

description.en: Keiko Fukuda (Japanese: 福田 敬子, Hepburn: Fukuda Keiko, April 12, 1913 – February 9, 2013) was a Japanese-American martial artist. She was the highest-ranked female judoka in history, holding the rank of 9th dan from the Kodokan (2006), and 10th dan from USA Judo (July 2011) and from the United States Judo Federation (USJF) (September 2011), and was the last surviving student of Kanō Jigorō, founder of judo. She was a renowned pioneer of women's judo, together with her senpai Masako Noritomi (1913–1982) being the first woman promoted to 6th dan (c. 1972). In 2006 the Kodokan promoted Fukuda to 9th dan.[8] She is also the first and, so far, only woman to have been promoted to 10th dan in the art of judo.

description.en: Kenshiro Abbe was a prominent Japanese master of judo, aikido, and kendo. He introduced aikido to the United Kingdom in 1955, and founded the Kyushindo system.  Abbe was a graduate of the Budo Senmon Gakko, having studied judo and kendo there. Following an illustrious early career in the martial arts, he served in the Imperial Japanese Army before and during World War II. He then trained in aikido under its founder, Morihei Ueshiba, for a decade. Abbe held dan ranks in several martial arts, most notably 8th dan in judo, 6th dan in aikido, and 6th dan in kendo. After introducing aikido to the UK, he established several Japanese martial arts councils there during the late 1950s. He returned to Japan in 1964 and remained there for most of the remainder of his life.

That early encounter with philosophy would be influential in the formation of his system. While the training was arduous at the Busen, Kenshiro managed to receive his Yondan (4th Dan) rank in Judo, being again the young Judoka to attain it. sources.cite: Tópico Bubishi (Judo Tradicional Goshinjutsukan)
sources.quotation: ...O que sabemos de fato é que, Maeda ensinou Judô a Carlos Gracie em virtude da afinidade com seu pai, Gastão Gracie. Carlos por sua vez ensinou a seus demais irmãos, em especial a Hélio Gracie. Neste ponto surgem duas teorias. A primeira alega que Maeda ensinou somente o judô de Jigoro Kano a Carlos, e esse o repassou a Hélio, que era o mais franzino dos Gracie, adaptando-o com grande enfoque no Ne-waza - técnicas de solo do judô, ponto central do Gracie jiu-jitsu ou brasilian jiu-jitsu. Para compensar seu biotipo, a partir dos ensinamentos de Carlos, Hélio aprimorou a parte de solo pelo uso do dispositivo de alavanca, dando-lhe a força extra que o mesmo não dispunha. A segunda teoria, apoiada pelos Gracies, fala que Maeda era, também, exímio praticante de Ju-jutsu tradicional e foi essa a arte que ensinou aos brasileiros. sources.cite: Russian Wikipedia - Kharlampiyev biography
sources.quotation: В 1936 г. окончил Государственный центральный ордена Ленина институт физической культуры (отделение дзюдо Василия Сергеевича Ощепкова)[...]Создавая «систему самбо», Харлампиев тщательно изучал дзюдо и осваивал его на практике. В дзюдо он видел основание нового вида борьбы в одежде, обогащённого наиболее эффективными приёмами других видов борьбы. Дзюдо он осваивал под руководством Василия Сергеевича Ощепкова, который во время многолетнего пребывания в Японии тренировался в школе дзюдо Кодокан.

sources.cite: Manual de Graduações e Regulamento de Graduações. Federação Portuguesa de Judo (Dezembro 2020)
sources.quotation: Em 1955, os judocas do Porto organizados em torno do professor Jackie Hugnet, criam o Círculo de Judo do Porto, onde Hugnet foi professor durante sete anos, lecionando três vezes por semana a primeira classe em que o Judo Kodokan foi ministrado de forma sistemática no Porto. Os professores Hugnet e Manuel Reis foram instrutores de Judo da Polícia de Segurança Pública do Porto, durante cerca de dois anos meio, coincidentes com parte do período em que o Comandante da corporação era o famoso Chefe Santos Júnior.

sources.cite: Manual de Graduações e Regulamento de Graduações. Federação Portuguesa de Judo (Dezembro 2020)
sources.quotation: No Verão de 1961, o professor Hugnet é substituído pelo também francês, Gilbert Bryskine, 4º Dan, campeão de França, bicampeão da Europa (1952 e 1954) e professor diplomado pela Federação Francesa de Judo e Ju Jutsu. É com Bryskine que os atletas do Círculo começam a participar em provas federativas, quer individualmente, quer por equipas. Em 1963, Gilbert Bryskine regressou a França devido a um grave acidente de automóvel que o deixou incapacitado.

sources.cite: José Branco não boicotou o seu sonho (Judo Magazine - Archived)
sources.quotation: O judo passou a ser central na sua vida que tinha levado uma volta muito grande. No Judo Clube de Portugal teve por mestre Kiyoshi Kobayashi e os seus colegas de clube passaram a ser os seus amigos para todos os momentos da vida quotidiana.

sources.cite: José Branco, Olímpico e Campeão de Tiro e Judo (The Delagoa Bay Company blog)
sources.quotation: Ao lado de josé branco, um amigo muito especial , mestre Kobayaschi . Refere o José: no período mais difícil da minha vida, então com 22 anos, quando me encontrava completamente atolado, foi o único que me lançou a mão. No último segundo da minha vida, ele fará parte dos meus pensamentos.

sources.quotation: Em 1958 o Mestre K.K. assinou então um contrato para ficar em Portugal por um período de dois anos. sources.cite: Ogawa Kinnosuke - Kenshi 24/7
sources.quotation: In 1905 a school was formally opened to teach kendo instructors and Naito was selected as the senior teacher. Kanō began studying with Iso, who had been a friend of Fukuda. Despite being 62 years old and standing only 5 feet (1.52 m) tall, Iso had gained a powerful build from jūjutsu training. He was known for excellence in kata, and was also a specialist in atemi, or the striking of vital areas. In Iso's method, one began with kata and then progressed to free fighting (randori). Kanō began training in Kitō-ryū with Iikubo Tsunetoshi (Kōnen). Iikubo was an expert in kata and throwing, and fond of randori. Kanō applied himself thoroughly to learning Kitō-ryū, believing Iikubo's throwing techniques in particular to be better than in the schools he had previously studied. sources.cite: Kenshiro Abbe, The Kyu-Shin-Do And Zen Judo - Keo Cavalcanti, 6th Dan Zen Judo
sources.quotation: At the Busen Abbe received instruction from Ogawa Hanshi (genius), the Butokukai Judan (10th Dan) sword master. While at the Busen Kenshiro also enrolled in Mr. Gen Tanabe's philosophy class, at the Kyoto Teikoku University. That early encounter with philosophy would be influential in the formation of his system. While the training was arduous at the Busen, Kenshiro managed to receive his Yondan (4th Dan) rank in Judo, being again the young Judoka to attain it. His sister, Toyoka, decided to take Martial Arts too, enrolling in Mrs. Mitamura's Naginata class. She would dedicate the rest of her life to the practice of the art.

sources.cite: Kenshiro Abbe, The Kyu-Shin-Do And Zen Judo - Keo Cavalcanti, 6th Dan Zen Judo
sources.quotation: In 1937, at the age of 23, Abbe was awarded his Rokudan (6th Dan) rank and in June of that year he enlisted in the Japanese army, serving for four years in a garrison in the Toan-sho Province in Manchuria. It was during the time in Manchuria that Abbe began formulating his theory of Budo (the Way of the Warrior), Kyu-Shin-Do. And it was also at this time that Abbe was invited by O'Sensei, Morihei Ueshiba to study Aikido under his care.

sources.cite: Tópico Bubishi (Judo Tradicional Goshinjutsukan)
sources.quotation: ...O que sabemos de fato é que, Maeda ensinou Judô a Carlos Gracie em virtude da afinidade com seu pai, Gastão Gracie. Carlos por sua vez ensinou a seus demais irmãos, em especial a Hélio Gracie. Neste ponto surgem duas teorias. A primeira alega que Maeda ensinou somente o judô de Jigoro Kano a Carlos, e esse o repassou a Hélio, que era o mais franzino dos Gracie, adaptando-o com grande enfoque no Ne-waza - técnicas de solo do judô, ponto central do Gracie jiu-jitsu ou brasilian jiu-jitsu. Para compensar seu biotipo, a partir dos ensinamentos de Carlos, Hélio aprimorou a parte de solo pelo uso do dispositivo de alavanca, dando-lhe a força extra que o mesmo não dispunha. A segunda teoria, apoiada pelos Gracies, fala que Maeda era, também, exímio praticante de Ju-jutsu tradicional e foi essa a arte que ensinou aos brasileiros. Porém, em uma recente entrevista, Hélio Gracie afirma que 'Carlos lutava judô', veja a entrevista http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BG309oqVLb4
